blocks.text: A 71-year-old retired seamstress sits on the edge of the bed in the morning, unable to bend her right hip far enough to put on her socks. The ache is worst after a day on her feet and eases when she sits. Her hip has been wearing out for a decade; whether it should be replaced depends on understanding what is wearing and why.

blocks.markdown: **Two broad families of joint disease.** *Osteoarthritis* (OA) is failure of articular cartilage with a mechanical, degenerative pattern: the cartilage thins, the subchondral bone thickens (sclerosis), bone cysts form and osteophytes grow at the margins. *Inflammatory arthritis*, of which rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is the commonest, is an immune-mediated synovitis: inflamed synovium (pannus) erodes cartilage and bone, and causes systemic disease. Both can end in arthroplasty, but the surrounding problems are different.

rows: Pain pattern
Mechanical: worse with use, better with rest; may be night pain late
Inflammatory: worse after rest, eases with movement
Morning stiffness
Brief, under about 30 minutes
Prolonged, over about an hour
Joints
Knee, hip, first carpometacarpal, distal interphalangeal joints; often asymmetric
Small joints of hands and feet (MCP, PIP, wrists), symmetrical; any joint
Examination
Bony swelling (Heberden's at DIP, Bouchard's at PIP), crepitus, reduced range
Warm boggy synovitis, ulnar deviation, swan-neck, nodules
Radiograph
Loss of joint space, osteophytes, subchondral sclerosis and cysts
Periarticular osteopenia, marginal erosions, uniform joint space loss
Blood tests
Usually normal inflammatory markers
Raised CRP/ESR; rheumatoid factor and anti-CCP often positive
Treatment
Exercise, weight loss, analgesia, injections, then replacement
Early DMARDs and biologics; surgery for damage
blocks.caption: Osteoarthritis and inflammatory arthritis compared

blocks.title: Worked example: two patients with hand pain
blocks.prompt: Patient A, 66, has pain and bony swelling at the distal interphalangeal joints of both hands, with stiffness for 15 minutes each morning. Patient B, 44, has swollen, warm metacarpophalangeal joints and wrists on both sides, with 2 hours of morning stiffness and a raised CRP. Classify each and decide what is needed.

steps.text: Patient A: distal joint involvement, bony nodules (Heberden's nodes) and brief stiffness are mechanical features of osteoarthritis. Treat with analgesia, activity advice and topical treatment; radiographs are not essential for the diagnosis.

Patient B: symmetrical metacarpophalangeal and wrist synovitis with prolonged morning stiffness and raised CRP suggests rheumatoid arthritis. Order rheumatoid factor, anti-CCP and radiographs of hands and feet.
Management for B: early referral to rheumatology for DMARDs. Surgery comes later, after irreversible damage.
Joint replacement is a late option in both and is considered once pain and loss of function persist despite conservative treatment.

blocks.answer: A has osteoarthritis (mechanical); B has probable rheumatoid arthritis (inflammatory) needing early rheumatology referral.

blocks.markdown: **Joint replacement.** Total hip and knee replacement are indicated when pain, stiffness and loss of function are substantially impairing life, and non-surgical treatment (analgesia, exercise, weight loss, walking aids, injections) is no longer enough. Surgery replaces the worn articular surfaces with a metal, ceramic and polyethylene bearing. Complications include infection (the most serious; may need revision), venous thromboembolism (thromboprophylaxis follows NICE and local guidance), dislocation (hip), loosening and wear, periprosthetic fracture, nerve injury and leg length discrepancy. Pre-operative optimisation addresses obesity, diabetic control, smoking and anaemia; in RA, additional issues are immunosuppressive drugs (managed jointly with rheumatology around surgery), steroid exposure and *cervical spine instability*: atlantoaxial disease can make neck extension during intubation dangerous, so cervical spine assessment is considered before general anaesthesia.

blocks.caption: $m$ body mass in kg, $h$ height in m; BMI in kg/m$^2$. Many units use BMI thresholds when planning elective arthroplasty; they differ between services.

blocks.markdown: **Low back pain and its red flags.** Most low back pain is non-specific, mechanical and self-limiting, and is managed with reassurance, staying active, analgesia and physical therapies, without imaging. The task is to find the minority with serious pathology. **Red flags** include onset under 20 or over 55 years, history of cancer, unexplained weight loss, fever or immunosuppression (infection), intravenous drug use, significant trauma or osteoporosis (fracture), constant night or rest pain, progressive neurological deficit, and features of cauda equina syndrome.

blocks.title: Cauda equina syndrome
blocks.text: In adults the spinal cord ends at about the L1-L2 level; below it the lumbar and sacral nerve roots run in the dural sac as the *cauda equina*. A large central disc prolapse (commonly at L4/5 or L5/S1), tumour or abscess can compress these roots. Suspect it with severe back pain, bilateral or alternating sciatica, saddle (perineal) numbness, new bladder dysfunction (altered urgency or sensation, then painless retention with overflow), bowel disturbance or incontinence, sexual dysfunction and reduced anal tone. **Emergency MRI and surgical decompression are needed**; once retention is established, recovery is worse, so recognise it early.

blocks.title: Checking the history
blocks.text: Ask every back pain patient about bladder, bowel, genital and saddle sensation. 'Do you feel the paper when you wipe?' and 'Can you tell when your bladder is full?' pick up early cauda equina when examination is still normal. A patient with a known cancer and new night spinal pain also needs urgent assessment for metastatic spinal cord compression.

blocks.markdown: **Septic arthritis** is bacterial infection of a joint, most often *Staphylococcus aureus*, arriving by the bloodstream, from adjacent osteomyelitis or by direct inoculation (surgery, injection). Risk factors: age, diabetes, rheumatoid arthritis, prosthetic joints, immunosuppression and intravenous drug use. A hot, swollen, very painful joint that the patient will not move, usually with fever, is septic arthritis until proven otherwise, because enzymes and pus destroy cartilage within days. Aspirate the joint (ideally before antibiotics unless the patient is septic and aspiration will be delayed), send fluid for Gram stain, culture, cell count and crystals, take blood cultures, and give IV antibiotics per local guidance (check BNF); surgical washout is usual. In children an *irritable hip* (transient synovitis) can mimic it; fever, inability to weight-bear and raised inflammatory markers favour septic arthritis, and validated clinical prediction rules exist.

blocks.title: Worked example: an adult hot knee
blocks.prompt: A 58-year-old man with rheumatoid arthritis on methotrexate has a hot, swollen, very painful right knee for 36 hours, with temperature 38.6 C and CRP raised. He holds the knee at 30 degrees of flexion. What do you do?

steps.text: Hot, swollen joint with fever in an immunosuppressed patient is septic arthritis until proven otherwise; rheumatoid flare and crystal arthritis are alternatives but cannot be assumed.

Take blood cultures and aspirate the knee under aseptic conditions: Gram stain, culture, cell count and crystals. Cloudy fluid with a high white cell count supports infection but counts overlap with other arthropathies, so culture and Gram stain decide.
Start IV antibiotics after samples (or immediately if septic) according to local guidance; hold or review methotrexate with rheumatology.
Arrange orthopaedic washout (arthroscopic or open), keep the joint rested, and monitor CRP; prosthetic joint infection would need specialist revision strategy.

blocks.answer: Presumed septic arthritis: aspiration, blood cultures, IV antibiotics and surgical washout.

blocks.markdown: **Developmental dysplasia of the hip (DDH)** is abnormal development of the acetabulum and femoral head, from a shallow acetabulum to dislocation. Risk factors: female sex, breech presentation, first-born, family history, oligohydramnios and tight swaddling with hips extended. Newborn and 6 to 8 week checks include the **Barlow** manoeuvre (adduct and push posteriorly to dislocate an unstable hip), the **Ortolani** manoeuvre (abduct and lift to relocate a dislocated hip with a 'clunk'), assessment of limited hip abduction and leg length difference. Ultrasound is the imaging of choice in early infancy (the femoral head is largely cartilage); pelvic radiographs are used from about four to six months. Treatment in infants is with a Pavlik harness; later presentation needs closed or open reduction. Missed DDH causes a limp, shortening and early osteoarthritis.

points: Osteoarthritis is a mechanical degeneration with brief stiffness and weight-bearing joint involvement; inflammatory arthritis causes prolonged morning stiffness, symmetrical small-joint synovitis and systemic features; replacement follows failure of conservative treatment.

Red flags in low back pain include age extremes, cancer, fever, trauma, night pain and neurological deficit; cauda equina syndrome (saddle numbness, bladder and bowel disturbance, bilateral sciatica) needs emergency MRI and decompression.

Septic arthritis (hot, immobile, febrile joint) needs aspiration, IV antibiotics and washout; DDH is detected by Barlow and Ortolani examinations and ultrasound and treated early with a Pavlik harness.
Antibiotic choices and thromboprophylaxis should be checked against current BNF, NICE and local guidance.

questions.stem: A 69-year-old woman has had right knee pain for four years, worse on stairs and at the end of the day, with morning stiffness lasting about 10 minutes and a bony, crepitant joint. CRP is normal. Which diagnosis is most likely, and which radiographic finding would support it?

options.text: Osteoarthritis; joint space narrowing with osteophytes
Rheumatoid arthritis; marginal erosions with periarticular osteopenia
Septic arthritis; periosteal reaction
Gout; punched-out lesions only

questions.correctOptionText: Osteoarthritis; joint space narrowing with osteophytes

distractorRationale.a: Correct: mechanical pain, brief stiffness and bony swelling.
distractorRationale.d: Acute attacks, not a chronic pattern.

questions.explanation: Mechanical pain, brief morning stiffness, crepitus and a normal CRP are typical of osteoarthritis. Radiographs show loss of joint space, osteophytes, subchondral sclerosis and cysts. Inflammatory arthritis would give prolonged stiffness, warmth and raised markers.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old woman with long-standing rheumatoid arthritis, on a biologic, is listed for total knee replacement under general anaesthesia. Which pre-operative consideration is particularly important in her condition?

options.text: Assess for cervical spine instability and plan peri-operative immunosuppression with rheumatology
No special preparation beyond an OA patient
Stop all analgesia a week before surgery
Exclude any chance of surgery until erosions heal

questions.correctOptionText: Assess for cervical spine instability and plan peri-operative immunosuppression with rheumatology

distractorRationale.a: Correct: atlantoaxial instability and drug management are specific issues in RA.
distractorRationale.b: RA has additional anaesthetic and drug-related risks.
distractorRationale.d: Erosions are irreversible; surgery is for damaged joints.

questions.explanation: Rheumatoid arthritis can affect the upper cervical spine, risking cord injury during intubation, so neck assessment is considered before general anaesthesia. Immunosuppressants and steroids need a planned peri-operative strategy with the rheumatology team.

questions.stem: Total joint replacement for osteoarthritis is normally considered when pain and functional impairment persist despite appropriate non-surgical treatment.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Arthroplasty is an elective option offered when conservative measures such as exercise, weight loss, analgesia and walking aids have failed and quality of life is substantially affected. It is not first-line treatment.

questions.stem: A 112 kg man of height 1.68 m is being counselled before knee replacement. Calculate his body mass index in kg/m^2.
questions.explanation: BMI = 112 / 1.68^2 = 112 / 2.8224 = 39.7 kg/m^2. Services use their own thresholds for optimising weight before arthroplasty, so the number should be interpreted with local policy.

questions.stem: A 44-year-old builder had a sudden onset of low back pain two days ago after lifting a paving slab. The pain is felt across the lower back, is eased by walking, and he has no leg symptoms, no sphincter disturbance, no fever and normal neurological examination. What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Reassurance, analgesia, staying active and physical therapy; no imaging
Emergency MRI of the whole spine
Strict bed rest for two weeks
Urgent spinal surgery referral

questions.correctOptionText: Reassurance, analgesia, staying active and physical therapy; no imaging

distractorRationale.a: Correct: non-specific low back pain without red flags.
distractorRationale.b: Reserved for suspected cauda equina or cord compression.

questions.explanation: Non-specific mechanical back pain without red flags is managed by reassurance, early return to normal activity, analgesia and physical or psychological therapies. Imaging is not indicated, and bed rest worsens outcomes.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman has had severe low back pain for two days. This morning she noticed numbness over the buttocks and between her legs, and she has not passed urine for 10 hours and does not feel the urge to. Anal tone is reduced. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Emergency MRI of the lumbosacral spine and urgent surgical decompression
Oral analgesia and review in two weeks
Lumbar plain radiographs and discharge
Pelvic ultrasound as outpatient

questions.correctOptionText: Emergency MRI of the lumbosacral spine and urgent surgical decompression

distractorRationale.a: Correct: this is cauda equina syndrome.
distractorRationale.b: Delay risks permanent bladder, bowel and sexual dysfunction.
distractorRationale.c: Radiographs cannot show nerve root compression.

questions.explanation: Saddle anaesthesia, bladder dysfunction and reduced anal tone indicate cauda equina compression. This is a surgical emergency: MRI and decompression should not be delayed, because outcomes are worse once retention is established.

questions.stem: List five red flags in a patient with low back pain and describe the features and management of cauda equina syndrome.
markingGuide: Red flags (any five): age under 20 or over 55, past cancer, unexplained weight loss, fever or immunosuppression, IV drug use, major trauma or osteoporosis, night or constant pain, progressive neurological deficit
Cauda equina compression of lumbosacral roots below the conus (about L1-L2) by central disc, tumour or abscess
Features: bilateral or alternating sciatica, saddle numbness, bladder disturbance then retention with overflow, bowel disturbance, sexual dysfunction, reduced anal tone
Poorer outcome once retention is established
questions.explanation: The marker looks for a clear list of red flags linked to the condition they suggest, and a precise description of cauda equina syndrome as an emergency with MRI and decompression. Good answers note that early features may be subtle.

questions.stem: A 4-year-old girl has had a fever for 24 hours and will not bear weight on her left leg. The left hip is held flexed and abducted, and any movement causes distress. CRP and white cell count are raised. What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Urgent ultrasound or aspiration of the hip, IV antibiotics and orthopaedic washout if confirmed
Reassure and give simple analgesia for a presumed irritable hip
Treat with a Pavlik harness
Discharge with outpatient physiotherapy

questions.correctOptionText: Urgent ultrasound or aspiration of the hip, IV antibiotics and orthopaedic washout if confirmed

distractorRationale.a: Correct: suspected septic arthritis of the hip.
distractorRationale.b: Fever and raised markers argue against transient synovitis.
distractorRationale.c: This is for infant developmental dysplasia.

questions.explanation: Fever, refusal to bear weight and a painful, restricted hip with raised inflammatory markers suggest septic arthritis, which can destroy the hip within days. Urgent aspiration, IV antibiotics and surgical drainage are required.

questions.stem: During assessment of a 14-year-old boy after late diagnosis of unilateral hip dysplasia, the right leg measures 85.5 cm and the left leg 88 cm from the anterior superior iliac spine to the medial malleolus. Calculate the leg length discrepancy in cm.
questions.explanation: Leg length discrepancy = 88 - 85.5 = 2.5 cm. The convention of measuring from the anterior superior iliac spine to the medial malleolus gives true length; apparent length measured from the umbilicus can differ because of pelvic tilt.

questions.stem: Describe the risk factors, examination findings and initial management of developmental dysplasia of the hip.
markingGuide: Risk factors: female, breech, first-born, family history, oligohydramnios, tight swaddling
Examination: Barlow (dislocatable), Ortolani (relocatable clunk), limited abduction, leg length asymmetry
Ultrasound in early infancy; radiograph after about 4-6 months
Pavlik harness in infants; closed or open reduction if late
Consequences if missed: limp, shortening, early osteoarthritis
questions.explanation: A good answer connects risk factors, the Barlow and Ortolani tests and imaging by age, and states that early treatment with a harness achieves the best results.
